desc:
Given an array nums of non-negative integers, return the second largest distinct value in it. Equal values count as one: in [9, 9, 5] the largest value is 9 and the second largest is 5.

If the array has fewer than two distinct values, return -1. Do it in a single pass without sorting.

Example: nums = [5, 3, 9, 9, 1] returns 5.
hints: Sorting works, but a single scan is enough. What do you need to remember about the elements seen so far?
Keep two variables: the largest value so far and the second largest value that is strictly smaller than it.
For each x: if x is bigger than the largest, the old largest becomes the second largest; else if x is strictly between the second and the largest, it replaces the second. Equal values change nothing.
editorial: Track first (the maximum seen) and second (the largest value seen that is strictly below first), both starting at -1. Because every input value is non-negative, -1 works as an 'empty' marker and is also exactly the answer to return when no second value exists.

For each x: if x > first, shift first into second and store x as the new first; otherwise, if first > x > second, store x as second. A value equal to first is skipped, which is what keeps duplicates from being counted twice.
This is one pass with two variables. Sorting would cost O(n log n), and a set plus sort uses O(n) memory for no gain.
